facts.statement: Liaoningosaurus is a basal ankylosaurid dinosaur from Liaoning Province, China.
facts.quote: Liaoningosaurus (meaning "Liaoning lizard") is an unusual genus of basal ankylosaurid dinosaur from the Liaoning Province, China

facts.statement: Liaoningosaurus lived during the Early Cretaceous, from approximately 125.4 to 118.9 million years ago.
facts.quote: that lived during the Early Cretaceous (late Barremian to early Aptian stages, ~125.4 to 118.9 Ma)

facts.statement: More than 20 specimens of Liaoningosaurus have been found, all representing juvenile individuals.
facts.quote: The type and only species, Liaoningosaurus paradoxus, is known from more than 20 specimens, represented by juvenile individuals.

facts.statement: Liaoningosaurus was named in 2001 by Xu, Wang, and You.
facts.quote: It was named in 2001 by Xu, Wang and You.

facts.statement: Preserved gut contents suggest Liaoningosaurus may have eaten fish, indicating it hunted or scavenged.
facts.quote: L. paradoxus was unusual among ornithischian dinosaurs in that it is speculated to have hunted or scavenged, with preserved gut contents showing that it may have eaten fish.

facts.statement: Some skeletal features suggest Liaoningosaurus may have been partially aquatic.
facts.quote: Additionally, some features of its skeleton may suggest that it was partially aquatic.

facts.statement: Liaoningosaurus is the oldest known ankylosaurid to possess a tail club.
facts.quote: It is the oldest ankylosaurid to have had a tail club

facts.statement: The species was formally described in 2001 by Xing Xu, Xiao-Lin Wang, and Hai-Lu You.
facts.quote: The specimen was named and described in 2001 by Xing Xu, Xiao-Lin Wang and Hai-Lu You.

facts.statement: The type specimen is a nearly complete skeleton measuring about 34 centimeters in length.
facts.quote: The type specimen, IVPP V12560, consists of a nearly complete, articulated skeleton measuring approximately 34 centimetres (1 ft 1 in) in length

facts.statement: The holotype was recovered from the Dawangzhangzi Bed of the Yixian Formation.
facts.quote: It was recovered from the Dawangzhangzi Bed of the Yixian Formation

facts.statement: A nearly complete skeleton was described in 2016 by Ji Qiang and colleagues.
facts.quote: In 2016, a nearly complete skeleton of Liaoningosaurus was described by Ji Qiang, Wu Xiaochun, Cheng Yennien, Ten Fangfang, Wang Xuri and Ji Yannan.

facts.statement: Specimen XHPM-1206 was collected from the Jianshangou Bed, approximately 160 km west of the holotype site.
facts.quote: The specimen, XHPM-1206, was collected from the Jianshangou Bed of the Yixian Formation, about 160 km west from the holotype locality.

facts.statement: A nearly complete skeleton was described in 2022 from the Jiufotang Formation in Liaoning Province.
facts.quote: In 2022, Chang-Fu Zhou, Qing Liu, Xinyue Wang and Honggang Zhang described a nearly complete, associated skeleton (PMOL-AD00105) of Liaoningosaurus from the Jiufotang Formation of the Liaoning Province, China.

facts.statement: The type specimen is estimated to be about 34 centimeters long.
facts.quote: The type specimen of Liaoningosaurus has an estimated length of about 34 centimetres (1 ft 1 in).

facts.statement: The largest known specimen measures less than 45 centimeters in total body length.
facts.quote: The largest specimen, GPMA-12-045, has a total body length of less than 45 centimetres (1 ft 5 in)

facts.statement: A juvenile skeleton from the Jiufotang Formation is estimated to be 30 centimeters long.
facts.quote: A juvenile skeleton from the Jiufotang Formation has a total estimated body length of 30 centimetres (11.8 in).

facts.statement: The premaxilla bears slender teeth with few denticles.
facts.quote: On each premaxilla, slender teeth with few denticles are present.

facts.statement: Approximately 10 maxillary teeth are present, likely due to the animal's juvenile status.
facts.quote: There are only approximately 10 maxillary teeth, which has been suggested to be due to its juvenile status.

facts.statement: The tooth crowns resemble those found in Crichtonsaurus or Crichtonpelta.
facts.quote: The tooth crowns are similar to those of Crichtonsaurus (or Crichtonpelta).

facts.statement: Liaoningosaurus is the oldest ankylosaurid known to have possessed a tail club.
facts.quote: Liaoningosaurus represents the oldest ankylosaurid known to have had a tail club.

facts.statement: While Liaoningosaurus had a tail club handle, it did not appear to have a tail club knob.
facts.quote: Although it possessed a tail club handle, it does not appear that a tail club knob was present.

facts.statement: The tail club handle consists of interlocking neural arches where prezygapophyses overlap adjacent vertebrae by at least 50% of the centrum length.
facts.quote: The handle consists of interlocking neural arches on the distal caudal vertebrae, and prezygapophyses that overlap with the adjacent vertebra by at least 50% of the centrum length.

facts.statement: Liaoningosaurus completely lacks body osteoderms except for a few sub-triangular plates near the neck and shoulder.
facts.quote: With the exception of a few sub-triangular plates found near the cervical and pectoral region, it completely lacks osteoderms on its body.

facts.statement: Researchers debate whether the ventral bony plate is a true bone or merely skin impressions with scales, as broken edges lack bony histology.
facts.quote: Arbour et al. (2014b) re-examined and reinterpreted the ventral plate as skin impressions, with the tubercles instead representing flat polygonal scales. This reinterpretation is based mostly on the broken edges not revealing any bony histology.

facts.statement: Early phylogenetic analyses loosely placed Liaoningosaurus into the family Nodosauridae.
facts.quote: Their phylogenetic analysis loosely placed it into Nodosauridae.

facts.statement: A 2011 cladistic analysis suggested that Liaoningosaurus is a basal member of the Ankylosauridae family.
facts.quote: A second cladistic analysis performed by Richard Thompson and colleagues in 2011 suggested that Liaoningosaurus is a basal ankylosaurid.

facts.statement: A 2022 study recovered Liaoningosaurus in a polytomy with Cedarpelta and Chuanqilong, forming a sister clade to both Ankylosauridae and Nodosauridae.
facts.quote: although a reduced strict consensus performed by Frauenfelder et al. (2022) recovered it within a polytomy, along with Cedarpelta and Chuanqilong, that is sister clade to both Ankylosauridae and Nodosauridae.

facts.statement: The proposed semiaquatic adaptation included a 'shell-like' ventral bony plate covering the entire underside of the torso.
facts.quote: This is due to the presence of a 'shell-like' ventral bony plate that would have covered the entire ventral surface of the torso.

facts.statement: A 2014 study reinterpreted the 'shell-like' ventral structure as skin impressions rather than a bony plate.
facts.quote: However, a study by Arbour et al. (2014b) examined the shell-like structure and reinterpreted it as skin impressions with no bony internal texture.

facts.statement: Researchers suggested Liaoningosaurus was carnivorous, citing fork-like tooth denticles, sharp claws, and fish found within a skeleton.
facts.quote: In addition to a semiaquatic lifestyle, the authors suggested that Liaoningosaurus was carnivorous based on the elongated and fork-like denticles of the crowns of the cheek teeth, sharp unguals on the hands and feet, and the presence of fish within the skeleton of the second specimen.

facts.statement: Arbour and Currie (2015) identified the type specimen as a juvenile based on unfused neural arches, small size, and lack of post-cervical osteoderms.
facts.quote: Arbour and Currie (2015) considered the type specimen to represent a juvenile individual on basis of unfused neural arches, small size and the absence of post-cervical osteoderms.

facts.statement: Ji et al. (2016) argued that Liaoningosaurus specimens were adults, citing unfused ribs and absence of a synsacrum.
facts.quote: However, Ji et al. (2016) argued that the holotype, and other specimens, instead represented adults due to the lack of fusion of the ribs to the vertebrae, absence of a synsacrum, and small stature of all known specimens.

facts.statement: A 2025 study concluded via bone histology that all known Liaoningosaurus specimens died under one year of age.
facts.quote: Zheng et al., (2025) concluded that all specimens of Liaoningosaurus found so far were under a year old at the time of their deaths through bone histology.

facts.statement: Liaoningosaurus specimens have been recovered from the Dawangzhangzi and Jianshangou Beds of the Yixian Formation.
facts.quote: Specimens attributable to Liaoningosaurus have been recovered from the Dawangzhangzi and Jianshangou Beds of the Yixian Formation, which is a part of the Jehol Biota.

facts.statement: The Yixian Formation is composed mainly of volcanic rocks including andesites, andesite breccia, agglomerates, and basalts.
facts.quote: The Yixian Formation is mainly composed of volcanic rocks such as andesites, andesitebreccia, agglomerates and basalts.

facts.statement: The Yixian Formation represents a freshwater lacustrine environment characterized by shallow lakes lacking rivers and deltas.
facts.quote: It represents a freshwater lacustrine environment, lacking rivers and deltas among other variable features of freshwater settings. Such environments lacking these features include shallow lakes.

facts.statement: The environment had a yearly average temperature of about 10 °C (50 °F) with distinct wet and dry seasons.
facts.quote: The yearly temperature averaged about 10 °C (50 °F) and was temperate, with distinct wet and dry seasons.

facts.statement: Dating estimates for the Yixian Formation range from approximately 125 to 120 Ma, with recent U-Pb zircon estimates between 125.755 and 124.122 Ma.
facts.quote: Previous dating using 40Ar-39Ar isotopes gave an age of approximately 125 to 120 Ma, although more recent estimates indicate an age of 125.755 ± 0.061 to 124.122 ± 0.048 ma by using U-Pb zircon.

facts.statement: One Liaoningosaurus specimen was retrieved from the Jiufotang Formation of the Jehol Group.
facts.quote: One specimen of Liaoningosaurus was retrieved from the Jiufotang Formation of the Jehol Group.

facts.statement: The Jiufotang Formation dates to the late Barremian and Aptian stages of the Lower Cretaceous, approximately 122.0 to 118.9 Ma.
facts.quote: Based on analyses using secondary ion mass spectrometry (SIMS) zircon U-Pb, the formation dates to the late Barremian and Aptian stages of the Lower Cretaceous period, approximately 122.0–118.9 Ma.
